etymology: Hebrew Pisgah; the height (a peak of Mount Nebo) from which Moses viewed the promised land he would not enter.
biblical_def: Pisgah was a height in the mountains of Moab, the top of Nebo, from which Moses was given to view the promised land at the end of his life. The LORD had told him he would not cross the Jordan because of his sin at Meribah, but said, "Get thee up into the top of Pisgah, and lift up thine eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and behold it with thine eyes" (Deut 3:27). At the last, "Moses went up... unto the top of Pisgah... And the LORD shewed him all the land" (Deut 34:1), from Gilead to the western sea; "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither" (Deut 34:4). There Moses died, and the LORD buried him in a valley in Moab, and no man knows his sepulchre. From Pisgah the servant of God saw by faith the inheritance he would not tread in this life. Pisgah stands in the dictionary as the height of seeing-from-afar, a witness to the seriousness of God's discipline even toward His honored servants, and a tender picture of faith that beholds the promised rest from a distance, dying in hope of the better country, content to see and salute the promises afar off though not to enter them in this life.
webster_summary: The height (a peak of Nebo) from which Moses, barred for his sin, viewed the promised land before dying (Deut 3:27; 34:1-4); a picture of faith that beholds the inheritance from afar.

corruption_summary: Pisgah needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the seriousness of God's discipline toward His servants and the faith that beholds the promised inheritance from afar.
corruption_paragraphs: Discipline-denied correction. Some imagine that great usefulness exempts a servant from the consequences of sin. Moses, the meekest of men and the LORD's faithful servant, was barred from the land for his failure at Meribah, and saw it only from Pisgah. The dictionary holds that God disciplines those He loves and honors, and that even forgiven sin may carry temporal consequence; the height of Pisgah is a sober witness that no rank in God's service places one above His holy government.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is faith that embraces the promises from afar. Moses died on Pisgah in hope, having seen the land he would not tread — a pattern of the saints who "died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off" (Heb 11:13). The dictionary commends this hope: the believer may not enter every promise in this life, but he beholds the better country from the heights of faith, salutes it, and dies content in the God who keeps His word beyond the grave.

etymology: Hebrew Hor; the mountain on the edge of Edom where Aaron the high priest died and was stripped of his garments.
biblical_def: Mount Hor was a mountain on the border of the land of Edom where Aaron, the first high priest, died at the LORD's command, his sacred office passing to his son. Because Aaron, like Moses, had rebelled against the word of the LORD at the waters of Meribah, the LORD said he would not enter the promised land. At Mount Hor, in the sight of all the congregation, Moses brought Aaron and his son Eleazar up the mountain, "and Moses stripped Aaron of his garments, and put them upon Eleazar his son; and Aaron died there in the top of the mount" (Num 20:28). The whole congregation mourned for Aaron thirty days. The transfer of the priestly garments from father to son upon the mountain showed that the office continued though the man passed; the priesthood did not die with Aaron. Mount Hor stands in the dictionary as the mountain of the first high priest's death, a witness to the mortality of the Aaronic priests, who could not continue by reason of death, and so a pointer to the better and unchangeable priesthood of Christ, who, "because he continueth ever, hath an unchangeable priesthood" (Heb 7:24), and ever lives to make intercession for His people.
webster_summary: A mountain on the edge of Edom where Aaron the high priest died and his garments passed to his son Eleazar (Num 20:22-29); a witness to the mortal Aaronic priesthood that points to the unchangeable priesthood of Christ.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the contrast between the dying priests and the ever-living Christ. The Aaronic priests "were not suffered to continue by reason of death" (Heb 7:23); Aaron himself died on Mount Hor, his office handed to another. The dictionary holds the better priesthood of Christ, who, because He continues ever, has an unchangeable priesthood and ever lives to intercede; no successor strips His garments, for He does not die, but is a priest for ever after the order of Melchizedek.

Office-over-man note. The transfer of the priestly garments from Aaron to Eleazar on the mountain shows that the office continued though the man passed. The dictionary holds the principle: God's appointed offices and ordinances do not depend on any one mortal servant; the priesthood, the ministry, the church itself outlive the individuals who serve them, for they rest on the purpose of God, fulfilled at last and for ever in the one Priest who never dies.

etymology: Hebrew Seir; the mountainous land of Edom, given to Esau and his descendants.
biblical_def: Mount Seir was the mountainous region south and east of the Dead Sea, the land given by God to Esau and his descendants, the Edomites. "Thus dwelt Esau in mount Seir: Esau is Edom" (Gen 36:8). When Israel journeyed toward Canaan, the LORD forbade them to meddle with Edom, "for I have given mount Seir unto Esau for a possession" (Deut 2:5), and Israel passed by the borders of their kinsmen. Yet the long history between the brother-nations was bitter; Edom refused Israel passage, rejoiced over Jerusalem's fall, and was repeatedly denounced by the prophets, who pronounced God's judgment upon Mount Seir for its perpetual hatred and violence against Jacob (Ezek 35; Obad 1). In the days of Jehoshaphat, the LORD set ambushments against the invaders from Mount Seir, so that they destroyed one another and Judah needed only to gather the spoil (2 Chr 20:22-24). Mount Seir stands in the dictionary as the mountain-land of Edom, a witness to God's faithful apportioning of lands even to the nations outside the covenant, to the long and tragic enmity between Esau and Jacob, and to the certain judgment of God upon a people who nursed perpetual hatred against His chosen and rejoiced in their calamity.
webster_summary: The mountainous land of Edom, given to Esau (Gen 36:8; Deut 2:5); the home of Israel's hostile kinsmen, denounced by the prophets for their perpetual hatred of Jacob and judged by God (Ezek 35; Obad).

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certain judgment of God upon enduring hatred and rejoicing in others' calamity. Edom's sin was a "perpetual hatred" against its brother Jacob, and a malicious gladness at his ruin (Ezek 35:5; Obad 1:10-12). The dictionary holds that God marks and judges such settled malice; to hate one's brother, and to rejoice when calamity falls on him, is a grievous sin that does not escape the notice of the righteous Judge.

God's-ordering-of-nations note. God gave Mount Seir to Esau as a possession and forbade Israel to seize it. The dictionary holds that the LORD apportions the lands and bounds of all peoples, even those outside His covenant (Acts 17:26); His sovereignty governs the nations, and His faithfulness to His own promises does not cancel His just dealings with the rest of mankind, to each of whom He has appointed their place.

etymology: Hebrew Gilad; the highland region east of the Jordan, the setting of Jacob's covenant with Laban and Gideon's winnowing of his army.
biblical_def: Mount Gilead, or the highland of Gilead, was a fertile, mountainous region east of the Jordan, the scene of several significant events. There Jacob, fleeing from Laban, was overtaken; the two made a covenant of peace and raised a heap of stones as a witness, calling it Mizpah, "The LORD watch between me and thee, when we are absent one from another" (Gen 31:49). Gilead was famed for its balm, a healing resin (Jer 8:22, "Is there no balm in Gilead?"). And it was "from mount Gilead" that Gideon, by the LORD's command, sent home the fearful from his army, that the deliverance might plainly be God's: "Whosoever is fearful and afraid, let him return and depart early from mount Gilead. And there returned of the people twenty and two thousand; and there remained ten thousand" (Judg 7:3), and then God reduced them further to three hundred. Mount Gilead stands in the dictionary as the highland of covenant and of God's winnowing, a witness to the watchful LORD who keeps covenant between His people, to the famed balm that pictures the healing found only in God, and to the divine pattern of saving by the few, that no flesh might glory but the glory be the LORD's alone.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's saving by the few, that He alone may be glorified. At Gilead, Gideon's army was winnowed from twenty-two thousand to ten thousand to three hundred, lest Israel "vaunt themselves... saying, Mine own hand hath saved me" (Judg 7:2). The dictionary holds that God often reduces His people's strength to magnify His own, that no flesh should glory in His presence (1 Cor 1:29); the victories of faith are won not by numbers but by the LORD.

Balm-of-Gilead note. Gilead's famed balm became, in the prophet's lament, an image of a healing that the sin-sick nation would not seek: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" (Jer 8:22). The dictionary holds the deeper truth the image points to: there is a balm for the wounded soul, but it is found in God alone and supremely in Christ the great Physician; the tragedy is not the lack of remedy but the refusal of the sinner to come and be healed.

etymology: Hebrew Bashan; a fertile, mountainous region east of the Jordan, whose proud heights the psalmist contrasts with God's chosen hill of Zion.
biblical_def: Bashan was a fertile, well-watered region of high country east of the Jordan and north of Gilead, famed for its strong cattle ("bulls of Bashan") and mighty oaks. It had been the realm of Og, the giant king whom Israel defeated, and was given to the half-tribe of Manasseh. In Psalm 68 the high hill of Bashan stands as an emblem of proud, imposing mountains that look with envy upon the humble hill God chose for His dwelling: "The hill of God is as the hill of Bashan; an high hill as the hill of Bashan. Why leap ye, ye high hills? this is the hill which God desireth to dwell in; yea, the LORD will dwell in it for ever" (Psa 68:15-16). The towering hills of Bashan, for all their grandeur, were passed over; God set His love not on the loftiest peak but on Zion, the hill of His choosing. The hill of Bashan stands in the dictionary as the proud height that God did not choose, a witness that the LORD's election rests not on outward greatness or grandeur but on His own sovereign good pleasure, and that He delights to dwell, not with the high and mighty, but with the humble place and the lowly heart that He has chosen for His own.
webster_summary: A fertile high region east of the Jordan, realm of Og; in Psalm 68:15-16 its proud heights envy the humble hill of Zion that God chose to dwell in — a witness that God's election rests on His pleasure, not outward grandeur.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the freeness of God's choice. The towering hills of Bashan, grander by far, were passed over; God chose the modest hill of Zion for His dwelling. The dictionary holds that the LORD's election rests not on outward greatness, merit, or impressiveness, but on His own sovereign good pleasure: "the LORD hath chosen Zion; he hath desired it for his habitation" (Psa 132:13), and He still passes by the mighty to choose the lowly.

Pride-rebuked note. The proud high hills are pictured as leaping in envy at God's choice of the humbler Zion. The dictionary holds the rebuke to all human pride of place and power: God resists the proud and gives grace to the humble (Jas 4:6); He chooses the weak and lowly things to confound the mighty (1 Cor 1:27), and the soul that would be His dwelling must come down from the heights of self-importance to the humble place where God delights to dwell.

etymology: Hebrew Abarim, "regions beyond"; the mountain range in Moab from which Moses viewed the land before his death.
biblical_def: The mountains of Abarim were a range in the land of Moab, east of the Jordan, including the peak of Nebo and its summit Pisgah, from which the LORD commanded Moses to view the promised land at the end of his life. "Get thee up into this mount Abarim, and see the land which I have given unto the children of Israel. And when thou hast seen it, thou also shalt be gathered unto thy people, as Aaron thy brother was gathered" (Num 27:12-13). It was a place of Israel's encampment in the wilderness journey (Num 33:47-48), and the appointed height of Moses' death. From Abarim, Moses, denied entrance for his sin at Meribah, looked across to Canaan and then was gathered to his people. The command came with a gracious provision: God told Moses to set Joshua over the congregation, that Israel "be not as sheep which have no shepherd" (Num 27:17). The mountains of Abarim stand in the dictionary as the range of Moses' last ascent, a witness to the ordered passing of God's servants and the continuance of His work, for the LORD did not leave His people leaderless but raised up Joshua to bring them in, that the death of the shepherd might not scatter the flock, but the work of God go on.
webster_summary: A mountain range in Moab (including Nebo and Pisgah) from which Moses viewed the land before his death (Num 27:12-13); where God appointed Joshua to succeed him, that Israel be not as sheep without a shepherd.

corruption_summary: Abarim needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the ordered passing of God's servants and His provision of new leaders, that His work and people not be left without a shepherd.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's care to provide shepherds for His flock. As Moses went up Abarim to die, his first concern was that the people not be left "as sheep which have no shepherd"; and God appointed Joshua. The dictionary holds that the Lord does not abandon His people when their leaders pass, but raises up others to carry on His work; the death of a great servant is not the death of the cause, for the work is God's, and He provides for its continuance.

Succession-ordered note. The transfer of leadership from Moses to Joshua at Abarim was orderly, public, and God-appointed, with the laying on of hands and the charge before the congregation. The dictionary holds the pattern: the work of God passes from hand to faithful hand by His provision, and the church is to commit its truth and ministry "to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also" (2 Tim 2:2), trusting the Lord of the harvest to raise up shepherds in every generation.

etymology: Hebrew Moreh; a hill in the valley of Jezreel by which the Midianite host camped before Gideon's three hundred routed them.
biblical_def: The hill of Moreh was a height in the valley of Jezreel by which the vast host of Midian was encamped when Gideon came against them with his greatly reduced band. "Then Jerubbaal, who is Gideon, and all the people that were with him, rose up early... the host of Midian were on the north side of them, by the hill of Moreh, in the valley" (Judg 7:1). The Midianites and Amalekites "lay along in the valley like grasshoppers for multitude; and their camels were without number, as the sand by the sea side for multitude" (Judg 7:12). Against that innumerable host God had whittled Gideon's army to three hundred men, armed only with trumpets, pitchers, and lamps. In the night, at the breaking of the pitchers and the cry, "The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon," the LORD set every Midianite's sword against his fellow, and the great host fled. The hill of Moreh stands in the dictionary as the backdrop of Gideon's victory, where an innumerable enemy camped against three hundred men, a witness that the LORD saves not by multitudes or weapons but by His own power through the few who obey, and that the most overwhelming host is nothing before the God who fights for His people.
webster_summary: A hill in the valley of Jezreel by which the innumerable Midianite host camped before Gideon's three hundred routed them (Judg 7:1, 12); a witness that the LORD saves by the few, not by multitudes.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is not bound by numbers. By the hill of Moreh an innumerable host camped against three hundred men with torches and trumpets; and God routed the multitude. The dictionary holds the confession of Asa, "it is nothing with thee to help, whether with many, or with them that have no power" (2 Chr 14:11); the LORD saves by the few as easily as by the many, that no flesh may boast and the victory be plainly His.

Means-of-victory note. Gideon's three hundred conquered not with swords but with trumpets, broken pitchers, and lamps, and the cry of the LORD's name. The dictionary holds the pattern: God often gives His people strange and weak instruments, that the power may be seen to be of God and not of man. The weapons of the church's warfare are not carnal but mighty through God (2 Cor 10:4), and the LORD delights to overthrow the mighty by the weak things He has chosen.

etymology: Hebrew Mitsar, "littleness, smallness"; a hill near the sources of the Jordan from which the downcast psalmist remembers God.
biblical_def: Mizar was a small hill in the region of the upper Jordan, near Mount Hermon, named once in Scripture in one of the most tender of the psalms of the cast-down soul. The exiled or distant psalmist, longing for the courts of God like a panting hart, resolves to remember God even from his far-off place: "O my God, my soul is cast down within me: therefore will I remember thee from the land of Jordan, and of the Hermonites, from the hill Mizar" (Psa 42:6). From that little hill, far from the sanctuary, in deep discouragement, he turns his thoughts deliberately to God, and preaches to his own soul, "Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted in me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him" (Psa 42:11). The hill Mizar, "littleness," fits the smallness and remoteness of the place from which faith reaches out to the great God. The hill Mizar stands in the dictionary as the place of remembering God in the downcast hour, a witness that faith does not deny the soul's distress but addresses it, choosing to remember God and to hope in Him from the small and far places of discouragement, and preaching to itself until the cast-down soul rises again to praise.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the discipline of remembering God in discouragement. From the little hill Mizar, far from the sanctuary and cast down within, the psalmist deliberately turns his thoughts to God: "therefore will I remember thee." The dictionary holds that faith does not wait for the gloom to lift before remembering God, but remembers Him in the gloom; the believer recalls God's character and works to his mind, and so finds hope (Lam 3:21), even from the small and far places of distress.

Preaching-to-self note. The psalmist does not merely feel his discouragement but addresses it: "Why art thou cast down, O my soul?... hope thou in God." The dictionary commends this holy self-counsel: the downcast believer is to take himself in hand, to question his despondency and preach the promises of God to his own heart, until the cast-down soul is lifted again to hope and praise. Faith talks back to feeling, and the hill Mizar is its schoolroom.

etymology: Hebrew Tsalmon, perhaps "shady"; a wooded hill near Shechem where Abimelech gathered boughs to burn the tower, and a height named in Psalm 68.
biblical_def: Zalmon was a wooded hill near Shechem, named in the grim account of Abimelech's destruction of the tower of Shechem and again in a verse of Psalm 68. After Abimelech, the wicked son of Gideon who had murdered his seventy brothers to seize power, put down a revolt in Shechem, the people of the tower fled into a stronghold; "and Abimelech gat him up to mount Zalmon... and cut down a bough from the trees, and took it, and laid it on his shoulder" (Judg 9:48), and so his men burned the tower with all within it. Soon after, Abimelech met his own end when a woman cast a millstone from a tower and broke his skull — the curse of Jotham fulfilled, and the murder of his brothers requited upon his head (Judg 9:53-57). Psalm 68:14 also names Zalmon: "it was white as snow in Salmon," an image of God scattering kings. Mount Zalmon stands in the dictionary as the hill of Abimelech's cruelty and approaching judgment, a witness that the LORD repays bloodshed and tyranny, that the wickedness of the violent returns upon their own heads, and that no usurper's power, however ruthless, can escape the just recompense of God.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the certain recompense of bloodshed and tyranny. Abimelech murdered seventy brothers to seize power and burned the tower of Shechem from mount Zalmon; soon a millstone broke his skull, and "God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech" (Judg 9:56). The dictionary holds that God is not mocked, and whatsoever a man sows he reaps (Gal 6:7); the violence and cruelty of the tyrant return upon his own head, for the LORD avenges innocent blood.

Curse-fulfilled note. Jotham, the one surviving brother, had pronounced a parable-curse upon Abimelech and the men of Shechem; at Zalmon and its aftermath, that curse came to pass exactly. The dictionary holds the lesson: the word of God's warning is not idle, and the judgments He threatens against the wicked surely come; what is sown in blood is reaped in blood, in God's own time, that men may know there is a God who judges in the earth.

etymology: Hebrew har Ephrayim; the central hill country of the tribe of Ephraim, the setting of many events in Israel's history.
biblical_def: Mount Ephraim, the hill country of the tribe of Ephraim, was the central highland region of Israel, the scene of a great many events through the periods of Joshua, the Judges, and the kingdom. There Joshua received his inheritance and was buried (Josh 24:30); there Deborah the prophetess dwelt and judged Israel under her palm tree (Judg 4:5); there lay Shiloh, where the tabernacle long stood, and Ramah, the home of Samuel; and there too occurred the idolatry of Micah and the dark events of the Levite's concubine in the days when there was no king in Israel (Judg 17-19). The hill country of Ephraim was thus a region of both faithful service and grievous failure, a microcosm of Israel's history. Its highlands held the heart of the nation's life and worship for generations. Mount Ephraim stands in the dictionary as the central hill country of Israel, a witness to the mingled record of God's people — the burial-place of the faithful Joshua and the seat of Deborah's judgeship, yet also the scene of idolatry and lawlessness when every man did what was right in his own eyes — and a reminder that the same land may hold both the noblest faith and the darkest sin, as the heart of the covenant people swung between devotion and apostasy.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the sober honesty of Scripture about God's people. Mount Ephraim held the grave of faithful Joshua and the seat of Deborah's wisdom, yet also Micah's idol-shrine and the lawless horrors of Judges 19. The dictionary holds that the Bible does not whitewash the covenant people: the same land and nation that produced great faith also fell into deep apostasy, and the record stands as both encouragement and warning, that we presume not, but take heed.

No-king note. The dark events in mount Ephraim are framed by the refrain, "In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg 17:6). The dictionary holds the lesson: where there is no acknowledged rule of God and His law, men descend into idolatry and lawlessness, each becoming his own authority. The remedy is the rightful King, foreshadowed in Israel's monarchy and fulfilled in Christ, under whose righteous reign alone the heart finds its true order.
